top_strength: Discovery on access and walk distance was genuinely excellent and is the part of this call worth copying. She used the school bus equivalent correctly ('one school bus is about 30-40 feet'), pushed until she had a real number on both ends, landed on a documented 200-250 foot estimate, and then tied it straight back to the estimate as the one factor that could add time. She also preempted the customer's unasked question about vehicle capacity well, volunteering the 26-foot box truck and confirming one trip would do it, and she covered the clock section completely and correctly: on-site start at contract open, 2.5 hour minimum, 15-minute increments after, closed with 'Does that make sense?'
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: you never gave the Save Your Ass speech, and this was the exact call that needed it. Jake told you he had already moved most of his stuff himself and then balked at the price — that is the setup for 'Jake, one thing that saves people the most money is prep before move day. Anything small enough to fit in your car, take a carload over beforehand. Boxes consolidated, drawers emptied, nothing loose — the faster the guys can load, the shorter the clock runs and the lower your bill. Does that make sense?' That single block could have both lowered his real cost and kept him on the phone. Second priority: you made no attempt to book and no attempt to save. When he said 'I think I might have called the wrong place', that is not the end of the call — that is where you say 'I hear you, and let's make sure we're comparing the same thing. That $505 is the full 2.5 hour minimum with two movers, and there's no deposit — nothing due today. If the guys finish inside the minimum that's all you pay. Want me to hold Tuesday for you while you think it over?' Third: run the agenda statement at the top every time — the roadmap, the 10-15 minutes, and 'sound good?' — and slow down on the clock and pricing block. He had to ask you to repeat yourself twice, and you said 'twenty and a half hours' and got his name wrong in the first thirty seconds. Those small clarity misses are what made a price-sensitive customer decide you weren't his company.
phone_presence_notes: Polite but mechanical — 'Mm-hmm', 'I understand', 'okay, no worries' and 'rest assured' recycled verbatim throughout with almost no variation, the customer's name used wrong, and both real emotional cues (the mattress worry and the closing price objection) acknowledged with a flat 'I understand no problem' rather than engaged with.
